transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-09-10 15:00 UTC | duration 62m
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (StellarAI ML Infra), Liam O'Connor (StellarAI Backend), Sara Kim (StellarAI Security)

[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a technical deep dive today, Diego's going to walk through the profiler outputs and kernel selection behavior between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM, and we've got the Stellar infra context from Priya and Liam.
[00:18] Priya: Thanks, yeah we wanted to understand where the hot spots are; our main goals are sub-20ms token latency p95 for short chat-ish prompts and cost per 1M tokens under our current budget, also we need to run in our VPC with HSM KMS.
[00:37] Diego: Great, quick agenda — profiling methodology, CUDA graph traces, per-kernel timings, KV cache warmup, batching and latency impact, quantization artifacts, and recommendations.
[00:52] Liam: Quick infra note, we're running 8xA100 80GB connected with NVLink, using NCCL for comms, and we have MPS disabled for isolation. We're testing a 7B and a 13B model.
[01:10] Diego: OK, first slide — how we collect traces: we instrumented runtimes with nvprof/cuProfiler, tensorboard traces from TRT-LLM and vLLM's internal timers, and custom CUDA graph hooks. Important caveat: clock drift can make absolute numbers off by ~5-10%.
[01:36] Priya: That's fine, we're mostly interested in relative differences and kernel hotspots.
[01:44] Diego: Right, on dtypes — FP16 vs int8 quant profiles. TensorRT-LLM benefits from TRT's fused attention kernels and matmul ops, often fewer kernel launches with graph capture. vLLM (PyTorch) shows more small kernels, less fusion, but sometimes better memory reuse for KV cache.
[02:15] [02:30] Diego: Here's a typical timeline for a single token on 13B FP16 short prompt: TRT-LLM avg per-token 12.6ms, vLLM avg 18.9ms under same settings. But p95 widens for TRT when batch packing increases because some fused kernels scale poorly with ragged sequences.
[03:05] Priya: Interesting — is that with CUDA graphs enabled?
[03:10] Diego: These numbers are with CUDA graphs enabled for TRT-LLM; vLLM's CUDA graph support is more experimental and we measured without graph capture in that comparison. When we enable CUDA graphs for vLLM (via torch.cuda.graphs) we see improvement but it's sensitive to input shapes.
[03:35] Liam: Can you expand on 'sensitive to input shapes'?
[03:39] Diego: Sure, CUDA graphs freeze the kernel sequence — if your batch has variable sequence lengths we need to pad or capture multiple graphs. That increases memory and complexity. TRT-LLM's graph capture is more integrated and can better amortize kernel launch overhead for consistent shapes.
[04:05] [04:20] Diego: Per-kernel flamegraph: attention (fused mha) is ~40% of time on TRT-LLM, GEMM matmuls ~30%, KV cache reads/writes ~10%, memory transpose/reshape ~8%, other overheads ~12%. vLLM breakdown: many more small kernels, attention split across softmax, scale, matmul — overhead ~25%.
[05:02] Priya: How about KV cache warmup? Our workload is chat where long context grows, do we see large penalties on initial steps?
[05:15] Diego: Yes, warmup costs exist — first few tokens pay for KV cache population and occasional cache compaction. On our traces, warmup adds 20-40ms per token for very long contexts before amortization. TRT's fused KV handling tends to be faster once warmed.
[05:44] Ava: Any notes on memory fragmentation or OOM issues when using int8 quantization?
[05:50] Diego: Int8 with range calibration helps but can increase scratch workspace for certain fused kernels; TensorRT's engines may allocate additional workspace for int8 optimized op — watch peak memory. vLLM quantized paths (bitsandbytes / QAT) have different tradeoffs; sometimes slower single-token latency but lower memory footprint.
[06:28] Sara: From security side, we need assurance on data-in-rest encryption for KV cache and audit logs if we run on our VPC. Is Redwood's private offering compatible?
[06:40] Ava: Yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations, and audit logs. We'll send the whitepaper.
[06:50] Diego: Back to batch sizing — we tested batch sizes from 1 to 64. Throughput scales well up to ~16-32 for 13B with TRT and CUDA graphs, after which diminishing returns and increased p95.
[07:22] [07:40] Diego: There's a sweet spot depending on target p95; for <20ms p95 you often need batch packing heuristics that prioritize smallest sequences or dynamic bucketing.
[08:00] Liam: On multi-GPU: how well do kernels scale across NCCL for KV cache sharding?
[08:08] Diego: NCCL does well for collective ops, but the KV cache sharding adds a cross-GPU latency for KV fetches on autoregressive sampling. We recommend model parallel layout where KV shards are colocated with compute to reduce cross-node fetches.
[08:35] Priya: Any observations about cudagraph warmup and memory when doing hundreds of different prompt shapes in prod?
[08:45] Diego: Yes — capture explosion. If you capture per-shape you'll allocate many graphs and some per-graph buffers. Our recommendation: canonicalize shapes (pad/truncate) for capture or use a small set of representative graphs and fall back to non-captured paths for rare shapes.
[09:10] [09:25] Diego: Quantization results: FP16 baseline, TRT INT8 yields 1.6-2.2x throughput improvement on some ops but variable accuracy regression on some LLM behaviors; need per-task evals. bnb 8-bit on vLLM reduces memory by ~30% but throughput gains are smaller.
[09:55] Priya: Did you run end-to-end evals for QA/LLM hallucination?
[10:02] Diego: We ran small eval sets; int8 introduced subtle probability shifts — recommend post-quantization evaluation and possibly mixed precision for sensitive tasks.
[10:18] Ava: On the ops side, anything about kernel launches causing CPU-side stalls?
[10:24] Diego: Yes, kernel launch overhead and CPU-GPU sync points are major contributors. CUDA graphs reduce launches. Also pinned memory transfers reduce overhead for host->device for inputs.
[10:45] [11:00] Liam: For our VPC setup with strict egress rules, any special notes about profiling — can we run Redwood probe agents in our VPC?
[11:10] Ava: We can run a private profiling agent in your VPC, it's part of Private offering; it sends only aggregated telemetry unless you opt-in to share traces. We'll coordinate with your Sec team.
[11:28] Sara: We need a data flow diagram and SOC2 documentation before we enable agent.
[11:35] Ava: Noted, we'll send those.
[11:40] [12:00] Diego: Let's look at a specific CUDA graph trace — you can see in this capture the fused attention reduces number of kernel launches from ~120 to ~18 per token. The big win is reduced PCIe/driver overhead.
[12:25] Priya: In multi-tenant hosted vs dedicated — is the kernel selection deterministic?
[12:31] Diego: Kernel selection depends on engine build and heuristics — TensorRT can pick different algorithms per engine build and device. We track kernel variants in our runtime and have engineered rollbacks for regressions.
[12:51] [13:10] Diego: On profiling anomalies — watch for convolution heuristics and cuBLAS autotune producing different choices that change latency; we sometimes pin algorithms for production.
[13:33] Liam: Regarding rolling upgrades, how do you validate that new kernel picks don't regress p95?
[13:40] Diego: We run canary tests with representative prompt sets and automated SLO checks; if regressions appear we rollback the engine and alert.
[13:58] [14:20] Diego: We recommend a pilot: capture 1k representative prompts from Stellar, run on your 8xA100 and our dedicated cluster, compare per-kernel profiles with and without CUDA graphs, with FP16 and INT8 profiles.
[14:45] Priya: Sounds good — we can gather prompts, but need to know how to mask PII.
[14:50] Ava: We'll provide a masking script and instructions.
[14:56] [15:10] Diego: A couple of gotchas: Triton-like orchestration layers add another abstraction layer, sometimes interfering with CUDA graph persistence. Also watch CPU affinity and cgroups — noisy neighbors can hurt latency.
[15:34] Priya: Any recommended tools for visualizing kernel timelines?
[15:38] Diego: Nsight Systems for timeline and CUDA Graph dumps, nvprof for per-kernel stat (deprecated but still useful), and our internal per-kernel flamegraph exporter (we'll share.)
[16:00] [16:20] Diego: On batching heuristics — adaptive packing based on seq-length percentiles reduces p95 by ~20% vs naive fixed batches in our tests.
[16:40] Liam: For our chat use-case, we mostly have short back-and-forth messages but occasional long contexts, so adaptive heuristics sound right.
[16:52] Diego: For long contexts, consider prefix caching and storing KV shards on high-speed NVMe with prefetching if you can't keep all cache in GPU memory.
[17:10] [17:25] Sara: From compliance, we need to know retention windows for KV cache and logs.
[17:30] Ava: We support configurable retention windows and can purge KV caches on demand for Private deployments. For Hosted we'll need an enterprise contract to change retention beyond defaults.
[17:44] Diego: One more perf note — attention kernel implementations differ: some use fused rotary embeddings in kernel to avoid extra transposes, which helps latency.
[17:58] Priya: Any rough guidance for target batch size for 7B vs 13B to hit our p95 goal?
[18:05] Diego: For 7B you can push slightly higher batch sizes; 13B we found batch 8-16 with adaptive packing often hits ~15-22ms p95 depending on prompts and whether graphs are enabled.
[18:30] [18:45] Diego: Packaging the artifacts — we'll send per-kernel CSVs, Nsight captures, and a recommended config file to replicate tests.
[19:00] Ava: Quick recap — Diego will share kernel flamegraphs + recommended batch/graph configs; Priya will send prompt sets; Ava will share security docs and pilot pricing. Next meeting to review benchmark results.
[19:20] Priya: Targeting a pilot kickoff next week if we can get files in time.
[19:30] Ava: Great, we'll follow up.

End transcript.
